name: Joshua
author: The book is named after Joshua son of Nun, from the tribe of Ephraim, who served as Moses' assistant and then led Israel's army after Moses died. Jewish tradition holds that Joshua wrote most of it himself, with the account of his death added afterward by the priests Eleazar and Phinehas. Many scholars instead think it was gathered and shaped centuries later, drawing on older records, lists and stories, as part of a longer history of Israel that runs from Joshua through Kings.
audience: If Joshua wrote it, the first readers were the Israelites who had crossed the Jordan with him and were settling in Canaan, the land promised to their ancestors. If it was shaped later, it was read by Israelites under their kings, or by exiles in Babylon who had lost that same land and were looking back on how it was first received.
era: The events take place in Canaan, roughly modern Israel and the West Bank, either around 1400 BC by the traditional reckoning or around 1250–1200 BC as many scholars suggest. Canaan was a patchwork of small walled cities, each ruled by its own king, loosely under the shadow of Egypt. Its people worshipped many gods, especially the storm god Baal. Archaeologists still debate how the evidence on the ground fits the book's account of these years.

notes.5:13: Jericho, an oasis town just north of the Dead Sea, is among the oldest inhabited places on earth; archaeologists still debate when its ancient walls fell.
notes.7:1: Ai's name means 'the ruin'; it is often placed at a site called et-Tell near Bethel, though that identification and its dating are debated.
notes.8:30: Mount Ebal overlooks Shechem in the central hills; a stone structure found there in the 1980s was identified by its excavator as an altar, though others disagree.
notes.9:1: Gibeon lay a few miles north of Jerusalem; excavations there uncovered jar handles inscribed with the town's name.
notes.10:1: The Book of Jashar mentioned here was an ancient collection of Israelite poems, now lost, which is also quoted in 2 Samuel.
notes.11:1: Hazor, in the far north, was the largest city in Canaan; excavations found it destroyed by a great fire in the 1200s BC.
notes.13:1: The five Philistine cities listed here lay on the southern coastal plain; the Philistines were sea peoples who settled there around 1200 BC.
notes.15:45: Jerusalem stayed in Jebusite hands until King David captured it around 1000 BC and made it his capital.
notes.18:1: Shiloh, in the hills of Ephraim, became Israel's main place of worship and remained so until the days of the prophet Samuel.
notes.19:40: The tribe of Dan's move north to capture Leshem, also called Laish, is told in fuller detail in Judges 18.
notes.24:1: Shechem, between Mounts Ebal and Gerizim, was where Abraham first built an altar in Canaan and where Jacob later bought land.

flags.problem: The scholarly theory described (often called the Deuteronomistic History) is usually said to run from Deuteronomy through Kings, not from Joshua through Kings. As written it slightly misstates the alternative view.
flags.suggestion: Say it was 'part of a longer history of Israel that runs from Deuteronomy through Kings', or simply 'from the end of Moses' life through the kings'.

flags.problem: The Book of Jashar is mentioned at Joshua 10:13, not 10:1. Verse 10:1 introduces Adoni-Zedek, king of Jerusalem. A reader on 10:1 would see 'mentioned here' and find nothing about it.
Joshua 15:45 is about Ekron and its villages. The Jebusites holding Jerusalem appears at 15:63. The note is attached to the wrong verse and would confuse a reader.
The five Philistine cities are listed at 13:3, not 13:1. The note says 'listed here', which a reader on the 13:1 verse will not see.
flags.suggestion: Move the note to 13:3, or reword it so it doesn't say 'listed here'.
